newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond volatilities flat to down.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. T-bond volatilities flat to down.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options were flat to down slightly as bond prices were firm in narrow ranges, traders said Friday.
Thursday's sharp decline in Treasury prices drove implied volatilities higher, but activity cooled notably on Friday.
"Volatilities have been pretty steady, basically unchanged on the day," one trader said.

Traders said they were a little surprised that volatilities had not picked up ahead of key economic data due next week, particularly December producer prices on Thursday and December unemployment on Friday.

"People are waiting for next week. I think there's a good chance volatility can go up into next week," one dealer said. Friday afternoon, the lead March U.S. Treasury bond futures contract was ahead trading around 111-20/32, bouncing between 111-13/32 and 112-03/32.
Traders said bonds backed off the 112 area on a U.S. magazine article speculating that the Federal Reserve may raise short-term rates a quarter point in early 1997.
"After seeing more about it (the article), it's not all that bearish," one trader said.
"It's really quiet right now," he said of trading.

One trader said volatilities typically begin to increase about a week before key economic data are released, but that after Thursday's activity many investors were taking a breather, which kept volumes low and volatilities under wraps.
"Yesterday we saw a lot of option selling and it looked like they were playing toward the short side," he said. "Now you're seeing some guys coming in and buying some back."
He said market participants did not appear to be taking directional positions although the sentiment appeared to be leaning toward the bullish side.
Implied volatilities for February and March T-bond futures were around 10.4 and 10.3 percent respectively, little changed from Thursday afternoon levels.
Shorter-end volatilities were down slightly, traders said.
Implied volatilities for March and June Eurodollar futures options were around 8.5 percent and 13.6 percent, respectively, little changed to slightly down from late Thursday levels, traders said.
"If you get a weakish number for employment, the market will go back up and volatilities won't really have much of a chance of going up," a trader said.
"It's a tough point to do anything unless you really have to or unless you want to hedge something," he said.
A few large institutions were spotted in the markets Friday, but traders noted that big trades were few and far between.
Among them, one institution bought 1,000 of the February T-bond 112/114 call spread and another firm had bought 1,000 of the March 118 calls.
